The Desert pocket mouse (Chaetodipus penicillatus) exhibits a basal metabolic rate of 22.4 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 22.4 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when measured at a body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], a value consistent with the elevated metabolic demands typical of small, arid-adapted heteromyids. This resting oxygen consumption, derived from flow-through respirometry trials on captive individuals, reflects the high energetic cost of thermoregulation in a species that inhabits thermally extreme desert scrublands. In comparison to the closely related Bailey's pocket mouse (Chaetodipus baileyi), from which birth-mass estimates are often extrapolated, the Desert pocket mouse maintains a relatively typical heteromyid metabolic profile despite its smaller body size. Field records also indicate that under stable thermal conditions, these animals face considerable daily energetic challenges, as they must balance foraging activity with the need to avoid excessive heat exposure during daylight hours. The physiological capacity to sustain such a metabolic rate at the recorded temperature underscores the species' adaptation to its xeric environment, where food resources are unpredictable and thermal refugia are essential for survival.

Reproductive output in the Desert pocket mouse is best characterized by examining both litter size and breeding frequency. Females typically produce litters containing 1 to 7 pups per litter [N_R_i = 1 to 7 pups per litter], a broad range that reflects variation in maternal condition and resource availability across the species' Sonoran and Mojave Desert range. Under the temperature regime typical of the active breeding season, approximately 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C], the maximum reproductive rate integrates this clutch size with the frequency of breeding events; females may produce up to three litters per year [F_R_i = up to three litters per year] when environmental conditions are favorable. This annual reproductive output, combining a moderate litter size with a relatively high potential for multiple litters, is a common strategy among small desert rodents that experience short windows of resource abundance following seasonal rains. The timing and success of each reproductive event are tightly linked to precipitation patterns, which influence the availability of seeds and green vegetation that sustain both the lactating female and her developing offspring.

Neonatal body mass at birth is quite modest in this species, with newborn pups weighing approximately 1.4 grams [Wwb = approximately 1.4 grams], a value extrapolated from measurements of the morphologically similar Chaetodipus baileyi due to the difficulty of obtaining direct birth-weight data from wild populations. This low initial mass is characteristic of altricial rodent neonates that undergo a rapid period of growth and development within the maternal burrow. By the time females reach their ultimate adult size, they attain a maximum recorded body mass of 22 grams [Wwi = 22 grams], although field surveys show adult females typically range between 11 and 22 grams depending on seasonal fattening cycles and reproductive status. The substantial increase from birth mass to adult mass highlights the intense nutritional demands placed on nursing mothers, who must convert ingested seeds into milk to support litter growth. This growth trajectory is also reflected in the relatively short developmental intervals that follow parturition.

The developmental chronology of the Desert pocket mouse is closely synchronized with the thermal environment, with several key milestones occurring under a characteristic temperature of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C]. Nursing pups attain nutritional independence through weaning at 25 days after birth [tx = 25 days after birth], a period during which they transition from an exclusive milk diet to solid foods, typically seeds cached by the mother at a temperature of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C]. Following weaning, the juvenile period extends until the onset of puberty, which is reached at 120 days after birth [tp = 120 days after birth] under these same thermal conditions at a temperature of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C]. This relatively prolonged interval to sexual maturity, compared to some other small desert rodents, may reflect the time required to accumulate sufficient body fat reserves to support the energetic demands of reproduction. The consistency of these developmental timings across captive and field studies suggests a genetically canalized life-history schedule, although some plasticity in response to food availability has been noted.

Gestation in the Desert pocket mouse lasts approximately 25 days [tg = approximately 25 days] when measured at a body temperature of 35.3 °C [T = 35.3 °C], a duration that falls within the 23- to 26-day range reported by field studies and captive breeding records. This relatively short gestation, combined with the modest litter size and the rapid developmental schedule described above, allows females to produce multiple litters within a single favorable season. The maximum recorded lifespan for this species is 2 years [am = 2 years] under the thermal conditions of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C], although most wild individuals likely succumb to predation or environmental stress well before reaching this upper limit, with the Animal Diversity Web reporting a typical longevity of only 1 year in natural populations. This short lifespan, paired with the high potential for annual reproductive output, aligns with the opportunistic life-history strategy observed across many small heteromyid rodents inhabiting unpredictable desert environments.
